Description: Castanea crenata, commonly known as the Japanese chestnut, is a small to medium-sized deciduous tree that can grow up to 15 m tall. It thrives in cool, non-calcareous soils and is primarily cultivated as an ornamental tree. Notably, it is resistant to chestnut blight, a disease that has devastated the American chestnut (Castanea dentata). Its leaves, measuring 8 to 19 cm in length, are alternate, oblong-lanceolate, serrated, and pubescent on the underside. They are dark green in summer and turn yellowish-bronze in autumn. This species is monoecious, meaning each tree bears both male and female flowers. The flowers appear in late spring (May–June) in catkins, which are aromatic and creamy white to yellowish. Male flowers are positioned toward the upper part of the catkin, while female flowers are found near the base. The tree produces edible chestnuts, typically enclosed in groups of two or three within spiny, dehiscent husks. As they ripen, the husks turn yellowish and split open, revealing the chestnuts inside. Due to their high tannin content, these chestnuts have a bitter taste and are less favored compared to other varieties.

Description: The American chestnut (Castanea dentata) is a large, fast-growing deciduous tree belonging to the Fagaceae family. Historically, it could reach up to 30 m in height and 3 m in diameter. American chestnut trees are monoecious, meaning each tree has both male and female reproductive parts. The flowers are staminate catkins, borne on a central axis measuring 5 to 10 inches in length, and are produced in clusters from the axils of leaves. The lower lateral shoots consist exclusively of male flowers, while the upper upright shoots bear male flowers at the top and female flowers at the base. This tree is native to eastern North America. Before being devastated by chestnut blight, a fungal disease, it was one of the most important forest trees throughout its range and was considered the finest chestnut species in the world.

Description: The Chinese chestnut, also known as Castanea mollissima, is a deciduous tree from the Fagaceae family that can grow up to 20 m in height. Its leaves are oblong to oval, mostly rounded or heart-shaped at the base, tapering to a short, slender point at the apex. The margins are set with triangular teeth. The Chinese chestnut is distinguished from other chestnut species by the pubescence on the underside of its leaves. This plant is monoecious, meaning it has both staminate (male) and pistillate (female) flowers on the same tree. Aromatic, creamy yellowish-white flowers appear in catkins in late spring. Male flowers are located at the top portion of the catkin, while female flowers are found near the base. These flowers are followed by edible chestnuts encased in spiny, dehiscent burs (2–3 inches in diameter), typically containing 2–3 nuts per bur.

Its leaves are oblong to oval, mostly rounded or heart-shaped at the base, tapering to a short, slender point at the apex. The margins are set with triangular teeth. The Chinese chestnut is distinguished from other chestnut species by the pubescence on the underside of its leaves. This plant is monoecious, meaning it has both staminate (male) and pistillate (female) flowers on the same tree. Aromatic, creamy yellowish-white flowers appear in catkins in late spring. Male flowers are located at the top portion of the catkin, while female flowers are found near the base. These flowers are followed by edible chestnuts encased in spiny, dehiscent burs (2–3 inches in diameter), typically containing 2–3 nuts per bur.

Description: The European chestnut, or Castanea sativa, is a robust tree mainly found across the Mediterranean region and can reach a height of 35 m. Chestnut is an economically important tree used for both nut and wood production. If the tree is wild, it has a compact, ellipsoidal crown, while grafted ones are wide and spherical. It has a moderately deep, extensive, and robust root system. In light or cultivated soils, the lateral roots spread across the entire area, while the growth of the taproot ceases as the crown stops growing in height. The leaves are simple, alternate, and deciduous, with some marcescence. They have a short petiole, broadened at the branch insertion. The blade is oblong-lanceolate, prolonged into a fine point with a symmetrical base, reaching up to 25 cm. The underside of the leaves is pubescent, and the margins are regularly saw-toothed. The color of the leaves varies according to the variety. This species is monoecious, meaning the same tree has both male and female flowers. The male flowers are grouped in clusters of 5–10, gathered in long catkins found at the ends of branches. Each male flower has 10–12 stamens. Female flowers are located at the base of the catkins and consist of a perianth with six bilobed lobes. The fruits are formed by achenes at the base of the catkins, grouped in sets of up to three and covered by spiny bracts. The achenes have a hard, reddish-colored covering, shiny on the outside and velvety on the inside, with each achene containing a seed.

Description: Castanopsis carlesii is a broad-leaved, evergreen tree species in the family Fagaceae, primarily distributed in southern and southeastern China, as well as in Taiwan. It typically occurs in subtropical evergreen broadleaf forests at elevations ranging from 300 to 1,500 meters. The species thrives in warm, humid environments and often plays a dominant or co-dominant role in native forest canopies. This medium to large-sized tree can reach heights of 20–25 meters, with a straight cylindrical trunk and a rounded to spreading crown. The bark is grayish-brown and becomes fissured with age. Leaves are alternate, leathery, oblong to elliptic, and dark green with a glossy upper surface and a paler underside. Margins may be entire or finely serrate, depending on age and growing conditions. C. carlesii flowers in spring, producing small, unisexual flowers arranged in catkin-like inflorescences. The fruits are enclosed in spiny cupules and mature in autumn, typically containing one or two edible nuts. These nuts serve as a food source for local wildlife, including birds and small mammals. Ecologically, Castanopsis carlesii contributes to forest biodiversity and plays a key role in soil stabilization and nutrient cycling. It is also valued in reforestation efforts due to its adaptability and ecological importance. Additionally, the hard, durable wood is occasionally used in construction and furniture-making, while some parts of the plant are studied for potential medicinal properties.

Description: Castanopsis eyrei is a broad-leaved, evergreen tree species in the beech family (Fagaceae), widely distributed in southeastern China, including provinces such as Fujian, Jiangxi, Zhejiang, and Guangdong. It grows predominantly in subtropical montane evergreen forests at elevations ranging from 400 to 1,800 meters. It is one of the dominant tree species in mature secondary forests and natural reserves, playing a foundational role in local forest structure and dynamics. This medium to large tree can reach heights of up to 30 meters. The trunk is straight and often cylindrical, with smooth grayish bark that becomes slightly fissured with age. The leaves are alternate, leathery, and oblong to elliptic in shape, with entire or slightly toothed margins. The upper leaf surface is shiny dark green, while the underside is lighter with visible veins. The species flowers in spring, producing male and female flowers on the same tree (monoecious), with male catkins more prominent. Fruits are small nuts enclosed in woody, scaly cupules that mature in autumn. The nuts are not commonly consumed by humans but are important for wildlife such as squirrels and birds. Ecologically, Castanopsis eyrei is a keystone species in subtropical forest ecosystems, influencing biodiversity, microclimate regulation, and soil development. Its dominance in many forest types makes it a critical indicator species for ecological studies and forest conservation in southern China. The wood is dense and durable, traditionally used for fuel and low-grade timber, although its ecological value far outweighs its commercial use.

Description: Fagus grandifolia, commonly known as the American beech, is a large deciduous tree species in the beech family (Fagaceae), native to eastern North America. Description:
Deciduous round-head tree, originally from Japan, up to 25 m high. This tree grows faster than most European oaks. It grows in any average, well-drained soil, and pH is not important.

Its alternate deciduous leaves are anywhere from 20 to 40 cm long and half as wide, greenish in summer and orange-amber to brown in autumn. The blade is obovate to narrow, pubescent but glabrescent, with a rounded base and a margin with a few wavy to rough striae on each side.

The lower parts of new branches hang 5 to 10 cm long male inflorescences with dense vellus hairs on the axis. On the other hand, female inflorescences erect themselves at the sides of the upper part's new branches with 3 to 5 female flowers.

These trees bear fruit from an early age. These fruits are acorns, which are in small bunches measuring 2 cm and are half-closed by the dome. The domes are covered with long, narrow scales that protrude or are bent backwards. The tree bears fruit from a very young age.

Ecologically, Quercus mongolica is a key species in temperate forests, contributing to habitat complexity and nutrient cycling. Its wood is strong and durable, used for furniture, flooring, and construction. The species also plays a role in traditional medicine in parts of its native range.

Description: Quercus rubra, commonly known as northern red oak, is a large deciduous tree species in the beech family (Fagaceae), native to eastern and central North America. It typically grows in well-drained upland forests, often dominating mixed hardwood stands at elevations up to 1,200 meters. This species can reach heights of 20 to 35 meters, with a straight trunk and a broad, rounded crown. The bark is dark gray to blackish with shallow ridges and furrows. Leaves are simple, alternate, and lobed with pointed tips, typically 7 to 11 lobes per leaf. The foliage turns bright red to orange in autumn, giving the species its common name. Quercus rubra produces monoecious flowers in spring; male flowers form catkins, while female flowers appear singly or in small groups. The acorns mature in about 18 months and are enclosed in a shallow, saucer-shaped cupule. These acorns are an important food source for wildlife such as deer, squirrels, and birds. Ecologically, Quercus rubra plays a crucial role in forest ecosystems by providing habitat and food resources. Its wood is valued for flooring, furniture, and veneer due to its strength and attractive grain. The species is also widely planted in urban and restoration settings.
